title: CBFC Takes a Red Pen to 'Supergirl': Muted Cusswords, a Deleted Middle Finger, and the Same Old Diaspora Question
excerpt: Milly Alcock and Jason Momoa's DC outing opens in India on June 26 — but the version playing in Mumbai isn't the one playing in Manhattan. After 'Superman' lost its kiss last year, the censor board is back, and NRIs are once again watching the uncut cut from their couches.
body:
Here we go again. A big DC tentpole lands at India's door, the Central Board of Film Certification clears its throat, and out come the scissors. This time it's **Supergirl** — Craig Gillespie's darker, battle-scarred take on Kara Zor-El, starring a magnetic **Milly Alcock** and a scenery-chewing **Jason Momoa** as the chaos-loving bounty hunter Lobo. The film flies into theatres worldwide on **June 26**. But the version Indian audiences will see has been quietly trimmed, muted and disclaimer-stamped before it ever reached the big screen.

<youtube>https://youtube.com/watch?v=s1-pfiVMKAs</youtube>

Let's go to the certificate. The CBFC passed *Supergirl* with a U/A 16+ rating — but only after a round of audio surgery. Per Bollywood Hungama, the words **'screwed,' 'b***h,' 'balls'** and **'wh**e'** were all flagged for deletion. (That last one, the outlet notes, appeared in a scene shown at an exclusive 30-minute Mumbai preview on June 20, uttered by the leads in a *comical* context — which is to say, hardly the stuff of moral collapse.) A middle-finger visual was ordered gone. The board also asked for the usual anti-smoking and anti-alcohol messaging to be slotted in. Once the changes were made, the film was cleared on June 23 with a final runtime of **109 minutes and 58 seconds**.

If this feels like déjà vu, that's because it is.

> "What kind of oversensitive morons are running the censor board? You think Indian audiences can't handle kissing?" — A viewer on X, after 'Superman' was censored in 2025

Rewind to last July. James Gunn's **Superman** — the film that launched this whole rebooted DC universe, and in which Alcock first appeared as Supergirl — lost 41 seconds in India, including two kiss scenes between Clark Kent and Lois Lane deemed "overly sensual," plus an eight-second middle-finger gesture from Guy Gardner's power ring, swapped for a tame two-second alternate. The cuts sparked a full-blown social media revolt. One widely shared post nailed the double standard: the board "would allow horrific scenes of violence… but won't allow consensual kissing in a U/A comic book movie," while Bollywood's own item numbers sail through untouched.

The pattern is now a genre unto itself. *Thunderbolts* arrived with five muted expletives. *Mission: Impossible – The Final Reckoning* had "obscene" language scrubbed. And in the most-mocked example of all, *F1* replaced a middle-finger emoji with a fist bump — a single edit that, as one critic put it, "totally changed the meaning and left the audience confused." Studios have started anticipating the red pen and self-censoring before submission; *Mickey 17* was reportedly modified pre-emptively.

Here's the part that stings for cinephiles, though: there's barely any recourse. The Film Certification Appellate Tribunal was dissolved in 2021, so a studio that wants to fight a cut has to go to the high courts — slow, expensive, and a nightmare for a Hollywood major trying to hold a synchronized global release date. Easier to mute the swear word and move on.

## The diaspora angle

And this is exactly where the NRI experience splits clean down the middle. An Indian-American family in Edison or a desi student in London will watch **the international cut** — every cuss word, every gesture, every frame intact — on the very same June 26 it opens, whether in a Regal multiplex or a few weeks later on **HBO Max**. Their cousins in Mumbai will watch a film that's been gently sanded down. Same superhero, two slightly different movies, separated by a censor's note. For the diaspora, it's a quietly recurring reminder of the cultural gap that streaming has otherwise done so much to close.

The irony, of course, is that none of this dented *Superman*, which still scored the biggest opening weekend for a DC film in India's history. Audiences showed up anyway, foul-gesture-free. *Supergirl* faces a steeper climb — Warner Bros. is reportedly scrapping for screens against the Akshay Kumar juggernaut **Welcome To The Jungle**, which has multiplexes prioritising its showcasing this week — but Alcock's harder, more haunted Kara (raised, per Gunn, amid loss on a drifting shard of Krypton) is the kind of fresh take that could find its people.

Uncut or trimmed, *Supergirl* is in theatres June 26. The only real question — as ever — is which version you'll be watching, and which side of the world you'll be watching it from.
